domain.title: Data Engineering
domain.why: This is the plumbing that moves data from where it's created to where it's used — and unlike a normal bug, a bad decision here doesn't just break one feature, it quietly poisons everything built on top of it for years. Data engineering sits right where distributed systems, storage, and 'what does this number actually mean for the business' all collide, which is why mistakes here are some of the most expensive ones to undo.

sections.note: the decisions you cannot undo cheaply

L0.body:
The ladder. Each rung removes one class of update anomaly:

  1NF   every column value atomic; no repeating groups
  2NF   1NF + no non-key column depends on part of a composite key
  3NF   2NF + no non-key column depends on another non-key column
  BCNF  every determinant is a candidate key

  OLTP:  orders(order_id, customer_id, ...)  JOIN customers(customer_id, city, ...)
  OLAP:  fct_orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_city, customer_segment, ...)

The OLAP row repeats city on every order. That is the point, not a mistake.

concepts.L1: 1NF through BCNF eliminate update anomalies. OLTP systems normalize; analytical systems deliberately denormalize because storage is cheap and joins are expensive at scale.
concepts.L2: The reason to normalize is write correctness, not elegance. Once a table is append-only and never updated in place, most of the argument for normalization evaporates — which is why analytical modeling looks 'wrong' to an OLTP practitioner.
concepts.L3: Normalization buys one thing: a fact is stored in exactly one place, so one UPDATE can never leave two copies disagreeing. That guarantee is only worth paying for if you issue UPDATEs. An analytical fact table is append-only: rows are inserted once and never edited, so the anomaly class 3NF prevents cannot occur, and the redundancy 3NF forbids costs only storage, which columnar dictionary encoding makes almost free. Concretely, a 200-distinct-value city column over 100 million rows plain-encodes to about 600 MB but dictionary-encodes to 100 million 8-bit codes, 100 MB, before any compression codec runs. You traded 100 MB against a shuffle join over a billion rows.

L4.prompt_tpl: A table has {n} million append-only rows and one denormalized attribute with {k} distinct values. Argue whether normalizing that attribute into a dimension is worth it, and state the one condition that would flip your answer.
L4.answer: Not worth it. With $k$ small the column dictionary-encodes to $\lceil \log_{2} k \rceil$ bits per row, so the redundancy costs almost nothing, while the join costs a shuffle over all $n$ million rows. The condition that flips it: the attribute is mutable and corrections must apply retroactively to history, which reintroduces the update anomaly normalization exists to prevent.
L4.explanation: The decision is not aesthetic. Normalization pays for itself exactly when in-place updates happen. On an append-only fact table with a low-cardinality attribute, dictionary encoding makes the duplicate storage negligible and the avoided shuffle is the whole win.

L4.prompt_tpl: A column has {k} distinct string values averaging {b} bytes, over {n} million rows. Give plain-encoded size and dictionary-encoded index size in MB, and the ratio. Answer with the dictionary-encoded index size in MB.
L4.answer: Plain is $n \cdot b$ bytes; dictionary indices are $n \cdot \lceil \log_{2} k \rceil / 8$ bytes. For $k=200$, $b=6$, $n=10^{8}$: 600 MB versus 100 MB, ratio 6. For $k=200$, $b=12$: 1200 MB versus 100 MB, ratio 12. For $k=1000$, $b=6$: $\lceil \log_{2} 1000 \rceil = 10$ bits, so 600 MB versus 125 MB, ratio 4.8.
L4.explanation: Dictionary width is $\lceil \log_{2} k \rceil$ bits, not bytes. The dictionary page itself is negligible: 200 entries of 6 bytes is 1.2 kB against 100 MB of indices. This is why denormalizing a low-cardinality attribute into a wide fact table is nearly free in columnar storage.

L0.body:
Kimball's four steps, in order, before any DDL:

  1. pick the business process   "checkout"
  2. declare the grain           "one row per order line item"
  3. identify the dimensions     date, customer, product, store
  4. identify the facts          quantity, unit_price, extended_amount

  CREATE TABLE fct_order_line (
    order_line_sk   BIGINT,        -- surrogate; the grain's identity
    customer_sk     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    quantity        INT,           -- additive
    extended_amount DECIMAL(18,2), -- additive
    unit_price      DECIMAL(18,2)  -- NON-additive: never SUM this
  );

concepts.L1: Kimball's star schema: a central fact table of measurements at a defined grain, surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive attributes. Snowflake schema normalizes the dimensions.
concepts.L2: Declaring the grain — exactly what one row of the fact table represents — is the first and most important step, and skipping it is the source of nearly every double-counting bug in analytics. State the grain in one sentence before designing anything.
concepts.L3: Why grain first, mechanically. The grain fixes the functional dependency between the fact primary key and every measure. Suppose you declare the grain as one row per order but then attach a shipping cost that is really per shipment, and one order ships in three parcels. You now have three rows sharing an order_id, each carrying the full order total. SUM(order_total) grouped by month triple-counts, and nothing in the schema flags it, because the DDL type-checks fine. The taxonomy that saves you is additive (safe to sum over every dimension), semi-additive (safe over all but time, like an account balance), non-additive (never summable, like a ratio or a unit price).

L4.prompt_tpl: A fact table is declared at grain 'one row per order' but an order can ship in up to {p} parcels, and shipping_cost is per parcel while order_total is per order. The team stores both in this table. Describe the reporting bug and the fix.
L4.answer: To carry per-parcel shipping the table must go to one row per parcel, so order_total is repeated on each of up to $p$ rows and SUM(order_total) overstates revenue by the average parcel count. The fix is two fact tables at two grains: one row per order for order_total, one row per parcel for shipping_cost, joined only through conformed dimensions, never directly.
L4.explanation: Two measures with different natural grains cannot share a fact table. The double-count is invisible to schema tests and to null checks; it shows up as revenue that disagrees with finance. Declaring the grain in one sentence first is what prevents it.

L4.prompt_tpl: {o} million orders, each shipping in an average of {a} parcels. The team put order_total on a per-parcel grain table. By what factor is SUM(order_total) inflated, and how many rows does the table hold? Answer with the number of rows in millions.
L4.answer: Rows equal $o \times a$ million and the inflation factor is exactly $a$. For $o=10$, $a=2.4$: 24 million rows, revenue inflated 2.4 times. For $o=40$, $a=3.0$: 120 million rows, inflated 3 times. For $o=10$, $a=3.0$: 30 million rows, 3 times.
L4.explanation: The inflation factor is the average fan-out from the declared grain to the true grain of the measure, which is why it is always exactly the average parcel count and never something subtler.

L0.body:
dim_customer, Type 2. One business key, many surrogate keys:

 cust_sk | cust_id | segment | valid_from | valid_to   | is_current
 --------+---------+---------+------------+------------+-----------
  9001   | C-17    | SMB     | 2024-01-01 | 2025-07-01 | false
  9002   | C-17    | MID     | 2025-07-01 | 2026-02-15 | false
  9003   | C-17    | ENT     | 2026-02-15 | 9999-12-31 | true

The as-of join every query must now write:

  JOIN dim_customer d
    ON f.cust_id = d.cust_id
   AND f.order_ts >= d.valid_from
   AND f.order_ts <  d.valid_to   -- half-open, or you double-count
L0.cloze:
Type {{c1::1}} overwrites. Type {{c2::2}} adds a row with validity dates. Type {{c3::3}} adds a previous-value column.

The Type 2 join needs the business key AND {{c4::the effective date range}}.
The range must be {{c5::half-open}} or a fact at the boundary matches two versions.

concepts.L1: Type 1 overwrites (no history). Type 2 adds a new row with validity dates and a current flag (full history). Type 3 keeps a previous-value column.
concepts.L2: Type 2 is what people mean when they say 'we need history', and it changes every join in the warehouse — you must join on the business key *and* the effective date range. Retrofitting Type 2 onto an existing Type 1 dimension is a genuinely painful migration.
concepts.L3: The cost of Type 2 is a range join, and range joins do not distribute the way equi-joins do. Take 5 million customers with an average of 3 versions each: the dimension is 15 million rows. Join a 1-billion-row fact table on cust_id alone and you get 3 billion rows, three times the input, with revenue triple-counted. The half-open interval matters too: if valid_to of one version equals valid_from of the next and both use closed bounds, a fact stamped exactly at the boundary matches two rows and that single customer's orders count twice.

L4.prompt_tpl: {c} million customers average {v} versions each in a Type 2 dimension. A team joins a {f} billion row fact table on the business key only, forgetting the date predicate. How many output rows, and by what factor is a SUM of a fact measure wrong? Answer with the number of output rows in billions.
L4.answer: Output rows are $f \times v$ billion and the measure is inflated by exactly $v$. For $c=5$, $v=3$, $f=1$: 3 billion rows, 3 times too high. For $c=12$, $v=2.5$, $f=4$: 10 billion rows, 2.5 times too high. The customer count $c$ does not enter the answer, only the average version count.
L4.explanation: Fan-out from a missing temporal predicate equals the average number of dimension versions per business key. Note that $c$ is a distractor: it changes the dimension size but not the inflation factor.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Type 2 dimension uses closed intervals: version 1 has valid_to = '{d}' and version 2 has valid_from = '{d}'. A fact row is stamped exactly '{d} 00:00:00'. What happens, and what is the one-character-class fix?
L4.answer: The fact matches both versions, so it is counted twice and attributed to two different attribute values at once. The fix is a half-open interval: store valid_to as the next version's valid_from and compare with order_ts >= valid_from AND order_ts < valid_to, so exactly one version matches every instant.
L4.explanation: Half-open intervals are the standard fix because they tile the timeline with no gap and no overlap. Closed intervals require an exclusive-end convention such as subtracting one second, which then breaks silently the moment your timestamps gain sub-second precision.

L0.body:
Three table types, and only three:

  hub_customer     ( customer_hk, customer_id, load_ts, record_source )
  link_order       ( order_hk, customer_hk, product_hk, load_ts, src )
  sat_customer_crm ( customer_hk, load_ts, hash_diff, name, segment )
  sat_customer_erp ( customer_hk, load_ts, hash_diff, credit_limit )

Hubs hold business keys. Links hold relationships. Satellites hold
attributes, one per source system. Every table is insert-only.

New source system arrives -> add a satellite. Nothing existing changes.
L0.cloze:
{{c1::Hubs}} hold business keys, {{c2::links}} hold relationships, {{c3::satellites}} hold attributes with history.
One satellite per {{c4::source system}}, and every table is {{c5::insert-only}}.
Adding a new source means {{c6::adding a satellite}}, changing nothing that exists.

concepts.L1: Hubs (business keys), links (relationships), satellites (attributes with history). Optimized for auditability and schema evolution rather than query convenience.
concepts.L2: Data Vault is a raw-layer pattern, not a serving-layer one. Querying it directly is miserable; it's meant to feed dimensional marts. Teams that skip that second step get an auditable warehouse nobody can use.
concepts.L3: The schema-evolution property falls out of the physical split. The attribute lives in a satellite keyed by the hub hash key, so a new source is a new table and the existing ones are untouched: no locks, no backfill, no coordination. The price is that reconstructing one logical entity requires joining the hub to every satellite with a window function picking the latest load_ts per hash key, then joining that to the links. hash_diff exists to make loads idempotent: hash the attribute tuple, and insert a new satellite row only when the hash differs from the current one, so re-running a load inserts nothing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Data Vault satellite carries a hash_diff column. Explain precisely what re-running the same {n}-row load twice does, with and without hash_diff.
L4.answer: Without hash_diff the loader compares nothing and inserts all $n$ rows again with a new load_ts, so every entity gains a spurious version and any as-of query sees a change that never happened. With hash_diff the loader inserts a row only when the hash of the attribute tuple differs from the current satellite row for that hash key, so the second run inserts zero rows. hash_diff is what makes an insert-only satellite idempotent.
L4.explanation: Insert-only does not imply idempotent. Idempotence needs a content comparison, and hashing the attribute tuple gives a fixed-width one that works regardless of column count or types.

L4.prompt_tpl: An analyst asks for a dashboard over {e} entities modelled in Data Vault, needing the latest attribute values and two relationships. Recommend an approach and justify it in terms of what Data Vault is and is not for.
L4.answer: Do not query the Vault directly. Build a dimensional mart from it: one query per entity resolving the latest satellite row per hash key, materialised into conformed dimensions and a fact table at a declared grain, and point the dashboard at that. Data Vault is a raw integration layer optimised for auditability and additive schema change; the serving layer is a separate deliverable, not an optional one.
L4.explanation: The most common Data Vault failure is stopping after the raw layer. The result is auditable, evolvable, and unusable, because every business question becomes a multi-way join with a window function per satellite.

L0.body:
s3://lake/
  bronze/events/dt=2026-09-01/...    raw, as-landed, never modified, never deleted
  silver/events/dt=2026-09-01/...    parsed, typed, deduplicated, conformed keys
  gold/daily_active/dt=2026-09-01/   business aggregates and marts

The invariant that gives the pattern its value:

  bronze is write-once. Silver and gold are FUNCTIONS of bronze.
    silver = f(bronze)
    gold   = g(silver)

So any bug in f or g is repaired by re-running, not by recovering a backup.
Land the raw payload as a string column plus ingest metadata; parse in silver.
L0.cloze:
Bronze is {{c1::raw, immutable, as-landed}}. Silver is {{c2::cleaned, conformed, deduplicated}}. Gold is {{c3::business aggregates}}.
The invariant: silver and gold are {{c4::functions of bronze}}, so any downstream bug is fixed by {{c5::reprocessing}} rather than by restoring a backup.

concepts.L1: Bronze (raw, immutable, as-landed), Silver (cleaned, conformed, deduplicated), Gold (business-level aggregates and marts).
concepts.L2: The crucial property is that Bronze is never modified. Every downstream error is recoverable by reprocessing from Bronze, which means your pipelines can be wrong without being catastrophic. Teams that transform on ingest lose this and cannot reprocess history.
concepts.L3: The thing being bought is a recovery boundary. If you parse and filter on ingest, the only copy of the payload you ever had is the parsed one, and a parsing bug discovered six months later is unrecoverable: the source system has rotated its logs, the API no longer serves that window, and the bad rows are all you have. Keeping bronze byte-identical to what arrived, plus ingest metadata (source, file, offset, ingest_ts), makes every downstream error a compute cost rather than a data loss. Price it deliberately with lifecycle rules to colder storage rather than by deleting, because the moment you delete bronze the entire property is gone.

L4.prompt_tpl: Storage for bronze is {t} TB and growing {g} TB per month; a manager proposes dropping bronze older than 90 days to cut cost. State what capability is lost and propose the alternative.
L4.answer: You lose the ability to repair any bug older than 90 days: silver and gold stop being reproducible and become the system of record by accident. The alternative is lifecycle transition to an archival storage class plus compaction of bronze into large Parquet or Avro files, which cuts cost by roughly an order of magnitude while keeping the data. Deleting is a last resort and should be driven by a retention policy, not by a storage bill.
L4.explanation: The medallion property is not that bronze is cheap, it is that bronze exists. Archive tiers preserve the property at a fraction of the price; deletion destroys it permanently and silently.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team writes parsed, filtered rows straight into silver and keeps no bronze. {m} months later they discover the parser dropped every event whose user-agent contained a specific byte sequence. Explain what recovery options remain.
L4.answer: Essentially none from the lake. The dropped rows were never stored, so the only sources are upstream: the producing system's own retention, the message broker if its retention exceeds $m$ months (it will not), or backups of the source database. Recovery therefore depends on a system the data team does not control, which is exactly the dependency bronze exists to remove.
L4.explanation: Transform-on-ingest converts a reversible compute bug into an irreversible data loss. The asymmetry is the whole argument: storage is cheap and bounded, upstream retention is not yours to set.

L0.body:
Three ways to make a stage idempotent, best first:

1. Partition overwrite, keyed by the input window.
     df.write.mode("overwrite")
       .option("partitionOverwriteMode","dynamic")   # only the dt values present
       .partitionBy("dt").save(path)

2. MERGE on a stable key.
     MERGE INTO tgt t USING src s ON t.id = s.id
     WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

3. Deterministic output paths: same window, same object name, same bytes.

Anti-pattern, and the framework default:
     df.write.mode("append").save(path)     # re-run = duplicates, forever
L0.cloze:
1. {{c1::Partition overwrite}} keyed by the input window.
2. {{c2::MERGE}} on a stable key.
3. {{c3::Deterministic output paths}}.

The anti-pattern is {{c4::append}}, because re-running a failed task {{c5::duplicates rows}}.

concepts.L1: Every pipeline stage should produce the same result when re-run for the same input window. Achieved via partition overwrite, merge on key, or deterministic output paths.
concepts.L2: If a pipeline is not idempotent, backfills are dangerous and every failure requires manual reasoning. This is the single most important design property in data engineering and it's rarely stated as a requirement upfront.
concepts.L3: The reason this is the load-bearing property is that every orchestrator retries. So each stage runs at-least-once whether you designed for it or not, and the only question is whether a second run is harmless. Append is not: a task that wrote 400 of 1000 files and then died leaves 400 orphan files that the retry will write again. Partition overwrite is: the retry replaces the whole partition, so partial output is invisible. Note the trap in Spark, where the default static overwrite mode deletes every partition under the table root rather than only the ones present in the dataframe, which turns a one-day rerun into a full-table wipe.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Spark job writes with mode('overwrite').partitionBy('dt') and no partitionOverwriteMode setting, backfilling a single day into a table holding {d} days. What happens?
L4.answer: Static overwrite is the default: Spark deletes everything under the table path and writes only the one day, destroying the other $d-1$ days. For $d=400$ that is 399 days deleted. The fix is spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode set to dynamic, or an atomic table-format operation such as Iceberg overwritePartitions or Delta replaceWhere.
L4.explanation: This is the highest-cost single misconfiguration in batch Spark, and it is silent: the job succeeds, the day looks right, and the loss is discovered when someone queries history. Table formats avoid it by making the overwrite a metadata commit scoped to a predicate.

L4.prompt_tpl: A stage consumes an event stream with no natural primary key and writes to a table read by {n} downstream jobs. Retries are guaranteed. Choose an idempotence strategy and justify it against the two you rejected.
L4.answer: Partition overwrite keyed by the processing window. MERGE is rejected because it needs a stable key and there is none; a synthetic hash of the payload collapses legitimately identical events. Deterministic paths are rejected because with no key you cannot guarantee the same input rows land in the same output file across runs when partition counts or task ordering change. Window overwrite needs only that the input window is replayable, which the stream gives you.
L4.explanation: Choose by what identity you actually have. A stable business key buys MERGE; a replayable window buys overwrite; neither buys deterministic filenames unless the shuffle is deterministic too, which it is not by default.

concepts.t: Star, Data Vault, or One Big Table

L0.body:
1e9 order lines, 5e6 customers, 60 customer attributes.

  STAR    fct(12 cols) + dim_customer(5e6 x 60)
          1 join; dim ~2.4 GB raw -> broadcasts fine
  OBT     fct(12 + 60 cols)
          0 joins; 60 low-card cols at ~2 B/row = 120 GB extra storage
  VAULT   hub + link + N satellites, each needing a
          "latest row per hash key" window. Never serve from here.

The number that decides it:
  dim broadcastable            -> star, keep the join
  dim in the hundreds of millions -> OBT, the join is now a shuffle
  sources arriving unpredictably  -> Vault raw + star serving. Both.
L0.cloze:
{{c1::Star}} pays a join and keeps attributes in one place.
{{c2::One Big Table}} pays storage and removes the join.
{{c3::Data Vault}} pays query complexity and buys auditability plus additive schema change.
The deciding number is whether the dimension is small enough to {{c4::broadcast}}.

concepts.L1: Three physical shapes for the same logical model. Star normalises attributes into dimensions and joins at read time; One Big Table denormalises them into the fact and joins never; Data Vault splits everything into hubs, links and satellites for auditability.
concepts.L2: The choice is a bet on one number: whether the dimension stays broadcastable. A 5-million-row dimension broadcasts and the star costs nothing; a 200-million-row one shuffles a billion-row fact table on every query, and that is when denormalising into One Big Table stops being lazy and becomes correct.
concepts.L3: Cost it out. Denormalising 60 customer attributes onto a billion-row fact adds about 2 bytes per row per column after dictionary encoding, since these are low-cardinality strings, so roughly 120 GB of extra storage, which is cheap and paid once. Keeping the star costs one join per query: with a 5-million-row, 60-column dimension at about 2.4 GB raw, Spark broadcasts it to every executor and the join is nearly free. Now grow the dimension to 200 million rows, about 96 GB, and broadcast is impossible; every query shuffles the billion-row fact by customer key, and the star has quietly become the expensive option.

L4.prompt_tpl: A fact table has {f} billion rows. Denormalising adds {c} columns that dictionary-encode to about {b} bytes per row each. The dimension has {d} million rows and {c} columns at about {w} bytes each. Give the extra storage for OBT and the dimension size, and say which shape you would choose. Answer with the extra OBT storage in bytes.
L4.answer: OBT extra storage is $f \cdot 10^{9} \cdot c \cdot b$ bytes; dimension size is $d \cdot 10^{6} \cdot c \cdot w$. For $f=1$, $c=60$, $d=5$: 120 GB extra versus a 2.4 GB dimension, which broadcasts, so keep the star. For $f=5$, $c=60$, $d=200$: 600 GB extra versus a 96 GB dimension, which cannot broadcast, so OBT wins despite costing more storage.
L4.explanation: Storage cost scales with the fact table and is paid once; join cost scales with the dimension and is paid per query. The crossover is the broadcast threshold, which is why dimension size, not fact size, decides.

L4.prompt_tpl: A company ingests from {s} source systems, adds roughly {n} new ones a year, and must be able to prove to an auditor what any record looked like on any past date. Recommend a layering and justify each layer.
L4.answer: Data Vault as the raw integration layer, dimensional marts as the serving layer. The Vault absorbs each new source as additional satellites without altering existing tables, and because every table is insert-only with load timestamps, the auditor's as-of question is answerable by construction. The critical follow-up is that the distribution is not stationary: a new app version, a regional outage or a client-clock bug shifts the tail without any pipeline change. So instrument the late counter and alert on its rate, because the bound you chose from last quarter's data is a hypothesis about this quarter's, and the counter is the only thing that tests it.

concepts.t: Batch as a special case of streaming

L0.body:
The same aggregation, two runners, one set of semantics:

  WHAT   SUM(amount)
  WHERE  GlobalWindows        <- batch: ONE window covering all time
  WHEN   AfterWatermark, which for a bounded source fires at end of input
  HOW    irrelevant: there is exactly ONE pane

Streaming is the general case; batch is the degenerate one:
  bounded input -> watermark reaches +inf at end of input
  one window    -> no early firings, no late data, no retractions

And the duality goes the other way:
  a TABLE is a stream of changes aggregated up to now
  a STREAM is the diff between successive table states
L0.cloze:
Batch is streaming with a {{c1::single global window}}, a bounded input, and one trigger at {{c2::end of input}}.
Because there is exactly {{c3::one pane}}, the accumulation mode never matters in batch.
The table-stream duality: a table is a stream {{c4::aggregated up to now}}; a stream is the {{c5::diff}} between successive table states.

concepts.L1: Batch is not a different paradigm; it is streaming with a bounded input and one global window whose watermark reaches infinity at end of input. Everything hard about streaming, out-of-order data and retractions, is what the bounded case removes.
concepts.L2: The practical payoff is that a correct streaming job is automatically a correct batch job, but not the reverse. Batch code habitually assumes it sees all input at once, so lifting it to streaming means adding decisions, windows, watermarks and lateness policy, that batch let you leave implicit.
concepts.L3: The duality is the load-bearing half. A table is a stream of change events folded up to the present, and a stream is the sequence of diffs between successive table states, which is exactly what CDC produces from a database and what a materialised view consumes. It also explains why Kappa is coherent as an architecture rather than merely fashionable: if the log is the source of truth and every table is a view over it, then reprocessing is just recomputing a view, not a separate batch system.

L4.prompt_tpl: Express a nightly batch job that computes daily revenue over {d} days of history in the four Dataflow dimensions, and say which dimension a streaming version would have to change.
L4.answer: What: SUM of amount. Where: fixed one-day windows in event time, or a global window per day-partitioned run. When: a single trigger at end of input, since the source is bounded and the watermark jumps to infinity. How: irrelevant, because there is exactly one pane per window. A streaming version changes When, from end-of-input to a watermark trigger with optional early and late firings, and consequently must specify How.
L4.explanation: Batch answers three of the four questions by default and never has to answer the fourth. That is precisely the set of decisions that becomes explicit, and therefore hard, in streaming.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team maintains a batch job and a streaming job computing the same {n} metrics, and they disagree by {p} percent. Use the duality to propose a resolution that does not mean rewriting both.
L4.answer: Express both as the same four answers and the divergence localises. Batch almost certainly uses a global or per-day window with all data present; the streaming job uses a watermark bound and drops or defers late data, which alone explains a small $p$. Make the streaming job the single implementation and run it over a bounded replay of the same input to produce the batch numbers, so one codebase serves both and drift is impossible by construction.
L4.explanation: This is Kappa argued from semantics rather than from tooling. The precondition is a replayable source with enough retention, which is the same constraint that decides Lambda versus Kappa.

concepts.t: Kafka transactions and the read-process-write loop

L0.cloze:
The idempotent producer dedups {{c1::retries}} using a producer id and per-partition sequence numbers, within one session.
Transactions make a set of writes across partitions {{c2::plus the consumer offsets}} commit atomically.
Consumers must set isolation.level to {{c3::read_committed}}, because the default is {{c4::read_uncommitted}}.

concepts.L1: Kafka's two distinct mechanisms. The idempotent producer removes duplicates caused by retries within one session using a producer id and per-partition sequence numbers; transactions make a set of writes across partitions, together with the consumer offsets, commit or abort atomically.
concepts.L2: Committing offsets inside the transaction is the part that makes the loop exactly-once, and it is the part usually omitted. If offsets are committed separately, a crash between the output commit and the offset commit reprocesses the batch and emits it again, so the transactional producer bought nothing.
concepts.L3: Trace the identifiers. The idempotent producer is assigned a producer id and attaches a monotonically increasing sequence number per partition; the broker remembers the last sequence it accepted and silently discards a duplicate retry. Transactions add a user-supplied transactional.id that survives restarts: on initTransactions the coordinator fences any older producer using that id by bumping an epoch, so a zombie instance of a crashed task cannot commit. Commit writes markers into every partition touched, and a read_committed consumer buffers records until it sees the marker, which is exactly why exactly-once adds latency proportional to the commit interval.

L4.prompt_tpl: A consume-transform-produce loop uses a transactional producer but calls consumer.commitSync() after producer.commitTransaction(). It crashes between the two, {n} times a week. Describe the observable effect and the fix.
L4.answer: The output is committed but the offsets are not, so on restart the batch is re-read, re-transformed and re-emitted inside a new transaction that also commits. Downstream sees duplicates, $n$ times a week, despite read_committed. The fix is producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction before commitTransaction, so offsets and output are one atomic unit, and removing the separate consumer commit entirely.
L4.explanation: Exactly-once here is a statement about a single atomic unit spanning the output and the input position. Any design that commits those separately has a window, and the window is hit at exactly the rate the process crashes.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain what the idempotent producer alone guarantees when a broker acknowledgement is lost and the client retries {r} times, and what it does not guarantee after a producer restart.
L4.answer: Within one session the broker tracks the last accepted sequence number per producer id and partition, so all $r$ retries of the same record carry the same sequence and only the first is appended; the rest are acknowledged as duplicates. After a restart the producer gets a new producer id with sequences starting again, so records re-sent by application-level replay are appended as new records. Only a transactional.id, which survives restarts and fences the old epoch, closes that gap.
L4.explanation: The distinction is session-scoped deduplication versus cross-session fencing. It is exactly why enable.idempotence being true by default is not the same as the system being exactly-once.

{{c4::Unaligned}} checkpoints store the in-flight records inside the checkpoint instead of waiting.

concepts.L1: Flink's checkpointing is Chandy-Lamport adapted to a dataflow DAG. Sources inject numbered barriers, each operator snapshots when it has seen barrier n on every input, and the union of those snapshots is a consistent global state.
concepts.L2: Alignment is what makes the snapshot exactly-once and it is also what makes checkpoints fail under backpressure. A slow channel delays the barrier, so faster channels stay blocked, which increases backpressure, which delays the barrier further. Unaligned checkpoints break that loop by putting in-flight records into the snapshot.
concepts.L3: Why alignment is required for exactly-once: the snapshot must correspond to a state in which every operator has consumed exactly the same prefix of every input. If an operator snapshotted after processing some post-barrier records from a fast channel, those records would be both inside the state and, on recovery, replayed from the source, applying twice. Blocking the fast channel until the slow one delivers its barrier is what enforces the common prefix. Unaligned checkpointing keeps the guarantee differently: it records the buffered in-flight records as part of the checkpoint, so recovery restores both the operator state and the exact channel contents, and no replay double-counts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A job's checkpoints take {t1} seconds when healthy and time out at {t2} minutes under backpressure, always failing at the same two-input operator. Choose between raising the timeout, enabling unaligned checkpoints, and switching to at-least-once.

Unaligned keeps exactly-once and removes the blocking, at the price of larger checkpoints that now carry in-flight records.
L4.explanation: The signature of alignment stalling is that checkpoint duration correlates with backpressure and localises to a multi-input operator, while healthy duration is small. That pattern points at alignment, not at state size or upload bandwidth.

L4.explanation: The buffered A records are not lost, only delayed by $d$. That delay is the entire cost of alignment, and it is unbounded in principle, which is why $d$ of 90 seconds turns into checkpoint timeouts.

concepts.L2: Backfills are the load test you didn't schedule — running 400 days concurrently will saturate whatever your pipeline touches. Limit concurrency explicitly, and design partitioned output so a backfill overwrites rather than appends.
concepts.L3: Run the numbers before the backfill, because the failure mode is not your pipeline failing, it is your pipeline succeeding and taking everything else down. concepts.L1: Records arriving after their window closed. Options: drop, route to a side output, or trigger recomputation of the affected partition.
concepts.L2: Silently dropping late data is the default in many systems and produces numbers that quietly disagree with the source of truth. At minimum, count what you drop and alert on it.
concepts.L3: There are three distinct settings and conflating them is the usual error. The watermark bound decides when a window's result is first emitted. Allowed lateness decides how long the window's state is retained afterwards, so that a late record can trigger a corrected re-emission; it costs state proportional to lateness times window count and it interacts with the accumulation mode, since the correction is either a delta or a restated total. The side output catches everything beyond allowed lateness. Only the third is free, and it is the one most pipelines omit, which is why the dropped-row count is usually unknown rather than merely large.

Allowed lateness $l$ keeps window state alive $l$ past the watermark so late events trigger a corrected re-emission; it costs state, not latency. An event arriving $a$ minutes late is included with a correction if $a \leq b + l$, and otherwise goes to the side output. With $b=2$, $l=10$, $a=7$ it is included; with $a=90$ against $b+l=12$ it is not.
L4.explanation: One is a latency knob paid by every record, the other a memory knob paid only by windows still open. Teams commonly raise the watermark bound, which slows everything, when they meant to raise allowed lateness, which slows nothing.

L4.prompt_tpl: Windows of {w} minutes with allowedLateness {l} minutes over {k} thousand active keys. Estimate how many windows per key are held open simultaneously and the state multiplier versus zero lateness. Answer with the number of open windows per key.
L4.answer: Open windows per key is about $1 + \lceil l/w \rceil$: the current one plus those retained for lateness. For $w=5$, $l=60$: 13 windows per key, so roughly 13 times the state of zero lateness, and at $k=500$ thousand keys that is 6.5 million live window entries. For $w=1$, $l=10$: 11 per key, 220 million entries at $k=20000$ thousand keys.
L4.explanation: Allowed lateness multiplies state by roughly the lateness-to-window ratio, so a one-minute window with an hour of lateness holds sixty-one windows per key. This is the usual cause of a streaming job whose state grows until it cannot checkpoint.

        max_retry_delay=timedelta(minutes=30),
        execution_timeout=timedelta(hours=2))

  2, 4, 8, 16, 30, 30 ...  -> 5 retries span 2+4+8+16+30 = 60 minutes

  headers={"Idempotency-Key": f"{dag_id}:{task_id}:{run_id}"}

Rules:
  - retry only TRANSIENT failures; a schema error retried 5 times

  - the key derives from the LOGICAL run, never from uuid4()
  - timeout must be shorter than the interval, or runs overlap
L0.cloze:
Retries make every task {{c1::at-least-once}}, so every task must be {{c2::idempotent}}.
Exponential backoff with base b and cap c gives delays {{c3::b, 2b, 4b, ... capped at c}}.
An idempotency key must derive from the {{c4::logical run}}, never from a random uuid, or the retry looks like a new request.
Execution timeout must be shorter than the {{c5::schedule interval}}, or runs overlap.

concepts.L1: Orchestrators retry, so every task effectively runs at least once and sometimes several times. The contract that makes this safe is idempotence for internal writes and an idempotency key derived from the logical run for external side effects.
concepts.L2: Retrying a deterministic failure is not neutral, it is an amplifier. A malformed schema or a missing upstream partition fails identically on every attempt, so five retries turn one alert into a one-hour outage with the same root cause and a much later notification.
concepts.L3: The key must be a function of the logical run, not of the attempt. If a task POSTs to a payment or notification API with a uuid4 idempotency key, attempt two generates a new key and the server treats it as a distinct request, so the retry duplicates the effect and the header provides nothing. Deriving the key from dag_id, task_id and run_id makes every attempt of the same logical run collide on the server side, which is the entire point. The second rule is about time: if execution_timeout exceeds the schedule interval, a slow run is still executing when the next fires, and two runs write the same partition concurrently.

L4.prompt_tpl: A task retries {r} times with exponential backoff from {b} minutes, capped at {c} minutes, and each attempt runs for {a} minutes before failing. Give the total time from first failure to final failure.
L4.answer: Delays are $b, 2b, 4b, \ldots$ capped at $c$, and there are $r$ delays plus $r$ further attempt runs. For $r=5$, $b=2$, $c=30$, $a=12$: delays 2, 4, 8, 16, 30 sum to 60 minutes, plus 5 attempts at 12 minutes is 60, so 120 minutes after the first failure. For $r=3$, $b=5$, $c=60$, $a=3$: delays 5, 10, 20 sum to 35, plus 9 minutes of attempts, so 44 minutes.
L4.explanation: The number that matters operationally is when the on-call alert fires, which is at the end, not at the first failure. Two hours of silent retrying on a deterministic error is why retry counts should be small and reserved for transient faults.

L4.prompt_tpl: A task sends a notification with an Idempotency-Key generated by uuid4() at call time, and retries {r} times. The upstream is flaky and about {p} percent of runs retry. Describe what recipients see and give the fix.
L4.answer: Each attempt sends a different key, so the server sees distinct requests and delivers a notification per attempt. About $p$ percent of runs produce two or more notifications, up to $r+1$ in the worst case. The fix is a deterministic key derived from the logical run, such as dag_id plus task_id plus run_id, so every attempt of the same run presents the same key and the server deduplicates.
L4.explanation: An idempotency key that changes per attempt is worse than none, because it creates the appearance of protection. The key must identify the logical intent, not the physical request.

  S3KeySensor(..., poke_interval=60, timeout=6*3600, mode="poke")
  # BETTER: frees the slot between checks
  S3KeySensor(..., mode="reschedule")
  # BEST: no slot at all; the triggerer waits
  S3KeySensor(..., deferrable=True)
  # BEST of all: event-driven, no polling
  raw = Asset("s3://lake/raw/events")

  ingest 40m + dedup 25m + join 55m + agg 30m = 150m -> start by 03:30
  slack = 30m -> ONE retry of the 25m step, and nothing else.
L0.cloze:
A {{c1::poke}}-mode sensor holds a worker slot for its whole timeout; {{c2::reschedule}} mode frees it between checks and {{c3::deferrable}} sensors hold no slot at all.
An {{c4::asset}}- or event-driven schedule removes the wait entirely.
An SLA is only meaningful against the {{c5::critical path}}: sum the stage durations backwards from the deadline and see what slack remains.

concepts.L1: Sensors wait for a condition before downstream work runs. How they wait decides whether they consume worker slots. An SLA is a deadline on the DAG's critical path, and it is only credible if the path's durations plus retries fit inside the slack.
concepts.L2: Sensor deadlock is a self-inflicted outage nobody plans for: enough poke-mode sensors waiting for upstreams fills every worker slot, so the tasks those sensors are waiting for can never be scheduled. The pool is full of things waiting for things that cannot start.
concepts.L3: Do the arithmetic backwards from the deadline. If the critical path is 40 plus 25 plus 55 plus 30, that is 150 minutes, so a 06:00 deadline means starting no later than 03:30 and the slack is whatever earlier start you can arrange. That slack is the entire retry budget: with 30 minutes of slack you can absorb exactly one retry of the 25-minute stage and nothing else, which tells you the retry configuration rather than the reverse. The stronger move is to delete the waiting: an asset- or event-driven trigger starts downstream when the producer declares completion, which removes both the polling cost and the fixed schedule offset that most SLA misses are actually made of.

L4.prompt_tpl: A DAG's critical path is {a}, {b}, {c} and {d} minutes, with a deadline at 06:00 and a start at {st}. Give total runtime, latest safe start, slack, and how many retries of the {b} minute stage fit. Answer with the total runtime in minutes.
L4.answer: Total is $a+b+c+d$. For 40, 25, 55, 30: 150 minutes, latest safe start 03:30, so a 03:00 start gives 30 minutes of slack, which fits exactly one retry of the 25-minute stage with 5 minutes to spare. For 20, 50, 35, 15: 120 minutes, latest start 04:00, a 02:15 start gives 105 minutes of slack, fitting two retries of the 50-minute stage.
L4.explanation: Slack divided by a stage's duration is that stage's retry budget, which is why retry counts should be derived from the schedule rather than copied from a template. A retries=5 on a 50-minute stage with 105 minutes of slack is decorative.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cluster has {s} worker slots. {n} DAGs each start with a poke-mode sensor waiting up to {h} hours for an upstream produced by another DAG on the same cluster. Describe the failure and give two fixes.
L4.answer: With $n$ greater than $s$, sensors occupy every slot and hold them for up to $h$ hours, so the producing DAGs can never be scheduled and the sensors wait for work that cannot start. The cluster deadlocks until the timeouts expire. Fix one: switch to deferrable or reschedule mode so waiting consumes no slot or frees it between pokes. Fix two: replace polling with asset- or event-driven scheduling so downstream is triggered by the producer.
L4.explanation: This is a resource deadlock, not a bug in any single DAG, which is why it appears only above a threshold ratio of sensors to slots and is often blamed on load. Deferrable sensors remove the resource from the cycle entirely.

  3 band     split P into b bands of r rows; P = b*r

Banding splits P hashes into {{c2::b bands of r rows}}; two documents are candidates if they match on all rows of {{c3::any}} band.
The candidate probability is {{c4::1 - (1 - s^r)^b}} and the threshold approximation is {{c5::(1/b)^(1/r)}}.

concepts.L1: Finding documents that are similar but not identical, at web scale. MinHash turns each document into a small signature whose per-position collision probability equals the Jaccard similarity; LSH banding turns that into a sublinear candidate search.
concepts.L2: The commonly quoted threshold $(1/b)^{1/r}$ is an approximation to where the S-curve is steepest, not to where it crosses one half. For $b=14$, $r=8$ it gives 0.719 while the actual 50 percent crossing is 0.685, so a pipeline tuned by the formula alone is more aggressive than intended.
concepts.L3: Both parameters do distinct work and the trade is explicit. Increasing $r$, the rows per band, requires more positions to agree, which sharpens the curve and raises the threshold; increasing $b$, the number of bands, gives more chances to match, which lowers it. So the false-negative rate on genuinely near-duplicate pairs at 0.9 similarity is under 0.04 percent, while half-similar pairs are admitted only 5 percent of the time and are then rejected by exact verification. The reason this is not optional at scale: all-pairs comparison over one billion documents is about $5 \times 10^{17}$ pairs, which no cluster will ever finish.

L4.explanation: When verification is cheap, bias toward recall by choosing a threshold below the target. Signature cost is $b \cdot r$ hashes per document, so 20 by 5 at 100 hashes is also cheaper to compute than 14 by 8 at 112.

concepts.L2: Fertility is a cost multiplier that compounds. If the corpus is 92 percent English, the merges overwhelmingly encode English subwords, so Devanagari or Cyrillic text falls back toward per-character or per-byte tokens. concepts.L2: Pinning the data is necessary and not sufficient. Two runs over the identical snapshot diverge if the shard count, the shuffle seed or the data-loader's interleaving differ, because the token order differs, and order is part of the training trajectory, not an implementation detail.
concepts.L3: Table formats give the primitive for free, since Iceberg and Delta already record an immutable snapshot per commit and support querying as of a snapshot id, so a run pins an integer rather than copying terabytes. The failure mode is maintenance: expiring old snapshots and vacuuming orphan files is required to control storage and metadata growth, and it silently deletes the data files an old snapshot referenced. Set snapshot retention from run retention, not from storage cost, and record decontamination inputs in the same manifest, since which evaluation suites were excluded is part of what the dataset is.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two runs use the identical snapshot id and identical filter and tokenizer hashes but produce different losses at step {s}. Name three things the manifest failed to pin.
L4.answer: Shard count, since a different sharding changes which documents are adjacent; shuffle seed, which sets the order within and across shards; and data-loader interleaving or worker count, which changes how shards are drawn under multi-worker loading. All three change the token order without changing the token set, and order is part of the optimisation trajectory. Packing and sequence-boundary policy is a common fourth.
L4.explanation: Dataset identity and dataset presentation are different things. Reproducibility needs both, which is why the manifest must include the loader configuration and not only the data pointer.

prereqs: Open table formats: Iceberg, Delta, Hudi
